title: Why You Should Ignore Difficult Students The First Week Of School e-first-week-of-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin cautions against a common instinct: seeking advance warning about which incoming students have behavior reputations and then pre-emptively seating or monitoring them differently. He argues this extra attention functions as labeling, signaling to the student that nothing has changed and that they're expected to misbehave again, which becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. He describes how labeled students recognize special treatment instantly, since they've experienced it their whole school careers, and resign themselves to living down to expectations. His recommended alternative is to treat every student — including those with reputations — with the same gentle kindness and normalcy as everyone else, effectively giving them a clean slate. Importantly, he clarifies this doesn't mean tolerating misbehavior; the classroom management plan still applies to everyone equally, just without singling anyone out in advance.
points: Seeking advance warning about "difficult" students and then treating them differently functions as labeling and often triggers the very misbehavior it's meant to prevent.
Labeled students recognize special treatment (front-row seats, extra reminders) instantly and resign themselves to living down to it.
The recommended alternative is treating every student, reputation or not, with identical gentle kindness from day one — a clean slate.
This approach does not mean ignoring actual misbehavior; the classroom management plan is still enforced equally for everyone.
quotes: But by doing so, you can actually trigger their misbehavior. You can cause these challenging students to jump right back into the same bad habits they struggled with the year before.
Because the extra attention, especially during the first week of school, is a form of labeling .
The truth is, labeling has a profound effect on individual behavior, more so than any other classroom variable .
